ac_coverage.criterion: The decoded document keeps exactly today's Go shape: objects map[string]any, arrays []any, string, bool, nil and *jsonvalue.Number. No new Value struct and no ordered member slices. Only Number's internal representation changes.

Number holds a small exact decimal inline: an int64 mantissa with no trailing zeros plus an int64 exponent. This makes 0.99, 0.01, 1.0 and 1e2 native and exact. A big.Int mantissa is used only when the digits do not fit in int64. The fast path allocates no big.Int, and float64 never decides any answer.

Number's public methods keep their behaviour: Decimal, IsInteger, Rat, Canonical, String, Cmp and equality. The canonical and original number text are byte-identical in every report. No public function or type of the root package changes.

Every guarantee from story 179 holds. Powers of 10 are never raised to a large exponent, Cmp aligns mantissas only within the digit cap, Rat() stays lazy and counted, and multipleOf keeps the exact decimal/modular method. The number digit and exponent caps and their LimitErrors are identical. The existing amplification and allocation-free-equality tests in internal/jsonvalue/number_test.go pass unchanged.
Mixed fast/big operands compare, test equal and hash exactly, so 1, 1.0 and 1e0 are equal. uniqueItems, enum and const deep equality give the same answers as today.

Each of the nine number rules has tests on the fast path, the exact big path and the boundary between them. The rules are type integer, multipleOf, maximum, exclusiveMaximum, minimum, exclusiveMinimum, enum, const and uniqueItems. Boundary cases include int64 max and max+1 mantissas, trailing-zero normalisation, and exponents at the caps. The tests include 0.3 multipleOf 0.1, exact comparisons on huge integers and 1.0 as an integer.
Results are identical everywhere: the valid/invalid answer, the flag, basic, detailed and verbose reports, and the library Result. All existing tests pass unchanged.

One regression test proves that every hostile-input limit triggers at exactly the same inputs as before, with the same error and exit code 2. The limits are nesting depth, input size, ref chain, evaluation-step charging, output units, report bytes and annotation count.
The compiled Schema stays immutable and safe for concurrent use. A test covers concurrent validation of documents with fast-path and big-path numbers, and passes under go test -race.

The project's benchmarks are run before and after on the same machine. Both sets go into docs/benchmarks.md, with ns/op, B/op, allocs/op and the retained-heap metric. The document scenarios show lower allocs/op or B/op and lower retained heap. No scenario's allocs/op or B/op increases, and no scenario is more than 10% slower.
docs/benchmarks.md records the CLI peak memory before and after for the 0.5 MB, 5.5 MB and 0.33 MB documents, for information only.
This story adds and changes no allocation-limit test.

adr.summary: Second pass: all previous findings are resolved. Number now stores the magnitude inline (a uint64 never above MaxInt64) with no trailing zeros, and falls back to big.Int only for wider mantissas. Valu

assumptions.text: number_test.go reads the private fields exp, ndig and text, so Number keeps those names.
decode.go needed no change: newNumber keeps its signature.
equal.go and multipleof.go were not touched; the former uses numEqual unchanged and multipleof.go is T3's scope.
The uniqueItems hash/key is Canonical() in uniqueitems.go, which is already exact, so equal.go needs no change.
I did not run the whole suite, only the internal/jsonvalue package.

multipleof.go left unchanged: its exact decimal/modular method lives in the keyword, and a fast-path shortcut is optional and not needed for the tests. This reading of the task's 'if' is mine; say if you want the shortcut added.

The bound rules (maximum, exclusiveMaximum, minimum, exclusiveMinimum) share one case table, boundCases, defined in maximum_numberpath_test.go. enum and const share equalCases, defined in enum_numberpath_test.go. All rules share the npValid helper defined in type_numberpath_test.go.

The pinned thresholds (depth 12, input size 74, steps 199, ref chain 5, output units 5, annotations 18, report bytes 636) were measured on the current code, after T1 and T2 changed the number storage. I did not run them against the pre-change code. I assumed number storage does not affect these limits, because step, unit and depth charging does not depend on how a Number is stored.
The CLI exit code 2 for limit errors was not re-tested here. I relied on the existing CLI limit tests and tested the library error only.

The 'before' set is the earlier 'Story 202 after' figures already in the file, from the same machine and method. I could not rebuild the old tree to re-run it, because the session may only touch its own worktree.

The retained-heap acceptance line is not met: it is unchanged. The decoder already built the compact number form when the baseline was taken, so the saving shows in validation allocations. The doc records this as measured.

CLI peak memory is not measured. The large documents are generated and uncommitted, and I could not write them to disk or run a before binary outside the worktree. The doc says how to measure it by hand with /usr/bin/time -l.
CLI/Errors reads +7.1% ns/op against a 'before' run that was unusually fast. The doc attributes it to spread between sessions, and it is under the 10% limit.
I added the new benchmark in a new file instead of editing internal/jsonvalue/bench_test.go, because existing test files must not change. It reuses heapAlloc from bench_test.go.

The 'before' tree was the old Number files placed in this worktree for a while, since the guard blocks writing outside it. All other files, including the new benchmark files, were the same in both runs, so the two sets compare like with like.
The guard does not allow environment variables, so the peak-memory test is switched on with a test flag (-args -peakmem).

I updated the six per-rule test files this story created by adding the cap cases. Every existing assertion in them is unchanged. The cap fixtures are in type_numberpath_test.go so the other rules can use them.
CompileOrder B/op went up by 89 bytes (0.04%). The before and after run ranges overlap, so this is noise, and the docs say so. Its allocs/op fell by 7.
